doc.title: Tony Parenti and Anthony Sbarbaro Interview, 1959-06-29

title: Red lantern fish fries, Italian music school, band parades and Mario Fanatza
summary: Remarks on race relations and the red lantern, Parenti's solfeggio lessons with Professor Taverno, the Italian band, Jack Laine parades, and hiring tuba player Fanatza for La Vida.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Picking up the horn: first instrument and the trombone

blocks.x: And all the white people that really opened their door and enjoyed themselves, paid a little amount, whatever it was. It wasn't much money. You know, people can't just... But there was never no dissension. No. Never none of that stuff. That's the ridiculous thing, that dissension for... My gosh, I can never... Well, take for instance, those boys just go out there and catch catfish. Catfish is the big type of fish that is the best fried fish. In fact, I still think catfish... You ought to know, because you're one of the cooks of that. Well, that's right. But the funny thing about it, I went in many of those fish fried places around downtown where I live, you know, around the French Quarter. There's a lot of colored folks where my father and I were all raised. There's all colored folks around in Dominguez. Now, that point of this condition, that shame that has to continue on. Here are, like for instance, you and I are up here. We're born and raised down south in New Orleans. Now, we have a job and we're playing with Red Allen or we're playing with Omar Simeon or we're playing with Edmund Hall. Or we're playing with any of our other boys that were born and raised in New Orleans. We play up there together. We all have the same thing in common. There's no... Why uphold that old-fashioned value? Because things are not the same. We don't have that bad and good in every race, creed, or color, so to speak. You've heard that expression where people hung a red lantern up and immediately thought it was the other side of the tracks of that. It was a place where people would have fished on tonight. You know, and there was never no... There was nothing else but a good time. There might have been a little error once in a while where some guy walked and you see that red lantern. This is a little cat house, you know. So he goes in there and he gets messed up and he says, no, it's a catfish fry. All right, good. That's a little sense of humor there. But, Tony, going back in that same little conception of time, when you went... Well, let's put it this way. This has been written up evidently quite a bit. Sometimes a little thing is... Let me break in there, Seth. All right. You all right? Listen, Tony. Yeah. A lot of this conversation is all right and everything else, but what we want to get in there is back some of your early background, your teaching, all that, et cetera. You mean very beginning, when I first started? As near as you can remember. Well, you know the funny thing about that, Tony? It's only of the last several years that I have been told, as well as I have been mentioned in many little articles, the fact that I am one of the unusual so-called musicians of the New Orleans jazz era, so to speak. The reason that they say that, like Leonard Feather mentioned in one of his... He finally closed after he writes about me, he said, one of the best musicians to him ever left New Orleans. Now, of course... He should put all around. That covers all of the facts, all of the fields. I always say I mention that only primarily because I suddenly realized he meant that I was a studied musician in conjunction with the other little efforts. But it had a reason. The Italian folks, especially my father and mother, as well as many other Italian families that migrated to New Orleans in the early 1900s and latter part of 1890, they were typically opera lovers. They loved opera. In fact, my mother used to sing so- We had the French opera there, huh? Yes, we had our French opera there. In fact, they used to go. Yeah. And believe you me, they couldn't afford it. They'd go up to the highest level up in the pit there for the smallest price, but they would go. Yes. So when this occasion came, where a professor from Italy arrived in New Orleans, he was a very graduate of the Conservatory of Milan, and he got into this quarters where all the Italians are, and that's in the French quarters. Decatur Street, Charter Street, and all around that section, around St. Mary's Church, around the Lurch Line, and Charter Street, if my memory is right. And they instigated a school of music. And they instigated a school of music, which all the parents all took their children to this school of music. And this professor was a studded instrumentation that he could teach any instrument. And for a small nominal fee, maybe $2 a month, we would take one or two lessons a week. And the money was turned into a fund, and out of the fund, they would give the professor enough money for himself, and the rest would go into a fund. And we would donate it to a studio, a so-called studio, in the yard of the St. Mary's Church by the church itself. You ever remember his name? Professor. Professor Ernest Taverno. Taverno. Yeah. I think I know his son. Yeah. I wasn't doubting. He was a very fine teacher. And thereby, I was one of the kids that went there. Yeah. Now, we're taking lessons by the old Italian's conception of legitimate ways, and that is solfeggio, which means you read your music and divide it with your hands and call the notes out, and you don't have an instrument. But you know, and eventually learn all the division and subdivision and the notes. And so, that's the way I started with this group. Incidentally, there were a few of the boys who parents could afford to buy them their instrument, and they would take their lessons with their instrument, as well as the solfeggio. But lots of us, including myself, only studied solfeggio because we couldn't afford to buy a used instrument. But the fun, after a lot of time, would develop to a certain amount of money, of which they would send to Italy for instruments for us, including uniforms. So, after, I would say, almost a year, we have developed that amount of money sent to Italy for the instruments and also uniforms. And then I got my first instrument. By that time, I knew everything there was about music. It was only a question of learning how to finger the instrument. And that is the way I started. And it wasn't too long afterwards that I became the, out of the clarinet section. It's a band. Don't forget, this is a brass band. There's a regular school brass band. Ten clarinets in there. That's right. I started off from the last clarinet, and I finally winded myself up playing the first clarinet, which meant I was very talented. A lot more than I thought I was. I didn't even know what talent I had, but I just happened to... Do you ever remember, you got to after that school age, which is your starting, do you remember the first band that you might have played with, whether it was what we call a spasm band, but the first band that you actually made a night's pay with, do you remember the leader's name or anything like that? Well, Tony, let me try to tell you, it wasn't too long after this big band, the Italian band was in rehearsing with the entire personnel of the groups and the kids, and even the fathers that used to play was a part of the band. So there, now, thereby, our first job that I made was with that band. Concert band. Concert band. I remember I'm on the fathers. We did the St. Joseph Day Parade, the Italian St. Joseph Day Parade, and we did a lot of the Italian festival parade. Then we finally got into the Mardi Gras. We got into the carnival. And that was my first money. As far as the money, it wasn't much. It was $4 or $5, but it was a big deal as far as I was concerned because that was the first time I ever brought my dad any money. Those carnival parades at the very first, when we were doing, that's Jack Lane that was the contractor then. There was a head man over him who used to ride a horse, and I forget his name. But nevertheless, Jack Lane would contract us, you know. And I remember we used to do five parades, and we'd get $15. That was a lot of money. But this contractor, whoever he was, I don't know his name. It's awful. He would ride around and make sure none of the fellas were getting out of step, and they weren't playing too hot. We used to really tear those horses and those boys carrying those, what do they call them, flambos today? They used to go crazy, you know, at some of them. You talk about horses, Tony. This, to me, I love all those guys. But we did a parade with this Italian band in Gretton, not Gretton, Louisiana. Yeah, the fire parade? Gretton, Louisiana. I don't remember what I, some Italian festival, some saint festival. We paraded on this road, Tony, and they had six horses with cops on, policemen. They were, they were the, leading, leading, leading. And we followed these horses, and the dust was five inches thick on that road. And these horses are kicking this dust up in us, and we're blowing and breathing. And believe you me, I never swallowed so much dirt in all my life. And we just kept playing until we stopped at a road somewhere where evidently there was, somebody knew, somebody lived at a house. And that was what they call a resting period. That's right. Now we get beer. Yeah, that's right. And all we want to drink or whatever, might have something to eat. And we freshen up a little bit. And then we go back again. And we're kicking about. Those horses kicked up that grunt and illusion. You had a dirt man. It was so thick, it looked like a cloud was on top of us. An incident that happened there on this horse issue was the great Henry Brunus, the trombone player. That's right. He had one habit. He would play his head off like George. And he would blow with his eyes closed. Now you're marching in a parade. You're marching in a parade. And the horses, as Tony says, you could be the band in the middle or back, but if you happened to be the one in front, you had horses. And he's closing his eyes and giving all he's got. And lo and behold, he jams right into those animals. They jams that trombone on their legs. And the horse ran away with this fellow on top. And it was an awful clamber. Yeah. You know, that's also happened in my Italian spasm band, too. The bass player, that tuba fellow, I don't remember his name. He played the tuba. And we got those musical lines. Musical lines. And he's reading this part like mad. And he finally, without us knowing, he walked right into a lamppost. At which he almost bent his horn up and he hurt his lip. It reminded me of that same incident. It was a true incident because, you know, a lot of musicians that play today with their eyes closed. But this Henry Brunus, he was one of the exceptions on trombone, too. Incidentally, Tony, while I'm thinking of it, in this Italian band, we had a bass player. His name was Mario Fanatza. He was a very impressive fellow for me because he played a tuba. And he had a big, fine, powerful tone. And he had been an ex-musician. So, when he joined up with our band, it was for the love of it and whatever little he could make out of it. But he was practically, in those days, you would call him a professional bass player. But he wasn't working in the bass value as a professional. He was doing odds and ends and other types of work. But this fellow, Mario Fanatza, was there. And, you know, I'm going to stretch it until I became on my own when I became a little popular, when I had my jazz band. We're passing a lot of time. And when I was offered the job at the La Vida Nightclub, which was on Burgundy between Canal and I was there. At that time, I was playing at the Liberty Theater. And one of the owners, there were three owners, came over to see me at the Liberty Theater and asked me what I'd go and play down there with a band, blah, blah. And I did. And the object was I wanted a sousaphone. Now, the reason I wanted a sousaphone, because I happened to have seen Paul Whiteman for the first time down there at the afternoon on St. Charles Street. And that sousaphone was very prominent. Yeah, very, very. And also all those saxes, which I've never seen or heard a lot of music like that. But when this job came up, the only person I remember was Mario Fanatza. So I did go down to look him up. And he lived down in the French quarters around Decatur Street near the French Market. And believe you me, he had a bunch of children. And he was a carpenter then of a trade. And I saw him. And I made the proposition to him. I says, Mario, I have a job at nighttime. And I says, to play bass, a sousaphone, something like that, the way I put it to him. And the job page, I don't remember whether it was $45 or $50 a week, which was a bad deal. At that time, sure. He says, Tony, I love to... ... ... ... ... ... ... ... ... ... ...
